name: RadarChart
intent: Several measures on one shape: each point of the web is a measure, each series an outline across all of them, so two things can be compared on every measure at once.
usage: Use RadarChart to compare a few things across the same handful of measures, like two plans on their feature scores, or this account against the average on six health measures. It is one component: pass axes, the points of the web clockwise from the top, and series, one entry per outline with one value per axis. The web has four rings by default; the outer ring is a round number past the largest value unless max names it. fill (the default) fills each outline as well as drawing it, which reads well for one or two series; turn it off past that. showScale writes the ring values up the first axis. Hover anywhere in the web or use the arrow keys and the nearest point answers with every series' value; the keys wrap round the web. See contracts/radarchart.json for the full contract. Inside a loading page it draws its own skeleton in place: the page says loading once (FormLayoutContext, which RecordPage, ListPage, FormPage and Dashboard set), and it takes no loading prop of its own. The title stands as a bar at the length its words will take and the drawing as a faintly framed box of bars at the chart's own height (BP COBALT "chart skeleton"), so the chart arrives where its bars stood.

label.note: Names the chart for screen readers and captions its data table, like Account health by measure.

title.note: Visible title over the chart. The screen-reader name still comes from label.

subtitle.note: A quieter line under the title, like Northwind Traders against the average.

showHeader.note: Turns the title and subtitle off when the Card or Section around the chart already says the same.

axes.note: The points of the web, clockwise from the top, like Billing, Usage, Support. Three at least; past about eight the names crowd each other.

series.itemShape: { name: string; values: number[]; intent?: ChartIntent }
series.note: One entry per outline, with one value per axis in the same order as axes. intent picks the colour; by default series take the kit's series order, pink, orange, gray, cyan, mint, green, olive, yellow and purple; red is the danger colour and is never handed out.

levels.note: How many rings the web has. The outermost is the top of the scale.

max.note: The value the outer ring stands for. Without it the scale rounds up past the largest value in the chart. Give it when two charts must be read against each other, or when the measures are scores out of a known top.

fill.note: Fills each outline as well as drawing it. Good for one or two series; past that the fills muddy each other, so turn it off and leave the outlines.

showScale.note: Writes the ring values up the first axis, so the web can be read without the tooltip.

showLegend.note: The keys for the series. Turn it off for a single outline the title already names.

legendPosition.note: Where the keys sit: under the web, over it, or in a column beside it.

animate.note: Fades the outlines in on first paint. Never plays when the person prefers reduced motion.

format.note: How values read in the tooltip, the ring labels and the table.

currency.note: The currency code for format currency.

height.note: Height of the drawing in px, the names around the web included. The web takes the shorter of the width and the height.

emptyLabel.note: What the chart says in place of the web when there are fewer than three axes or no series.

useWhen: A few things compared across the same handful of measures: two plans on their feature scores, an account against the average.
A profile people read as a shape, where the dent on one measure is the point.
Scores out of a known top, with max set so two charts can be read against each other.
doNot: Do not use it for measures in different units. Every point shares one scale, so money beside a percent is a lie.
Do not use it for a trend over time. Use LineChart.
Do not use it to rank values. The eye reads a radar as an area, not a length: use BarChart, which is easier to read exactly.
Do not put more than three series on it. Past that the outlines cross into noise; drop fill at two.
Do not use more than about eight axes. The names crowd and the shape stops saying anything.
Do not reorder the axes to make a nicer shape. The order is part of what the chart says.
Do not draw charts with loose SVG or a chart library. Use the kit charts.
Do not use raw hex; pick an intent.
a11y: A figure named by label. The web is hidden from screen readers; a visually hidden table holds every value, with the axes as rows and the series as columns.
The chart takes focus: the arrow keys move from point to point and wrap round the web (Home and End jump to the first and last), and show the same tooltip as pointing at it. Escape hides it.
The point under the pointer or the keys has its spoke drawn stronger and a dot on every series, so the point in question is never carried by colour alone.
Series come with a legend and the tooltip names each one, so colour is not the only way to tell the outlines apart.
Motion is subtle and optional (animate), and never plays when the person prefers reduced motion.
snippet:
<RadarChart
  label="Account health by measure"
  axes={["Billing", "Usage", "Support", "Adoption", "Payments", "Contract"]}
  series={[
    { name: "Northwind Traders", values: [82, 64, 91, 70, 88, 76] },
    { name: "Account average", values: [70, 72, 68, 65, 74, 69] },
  ]}
  max={100}
/>
